author: Grace Chen
title: Depression: Montreal Model Shows Effectiveness in Study
text:
MONTREAL, June 18, 2025 – A recent study by Montreal researchers reveals that the antidepressant effects of ketamine can be substantially extended when combined with a supportive therapeutic surroundings and regular psychotherapy.
Ketamine ‘s antidepressant effects can last up to eight weeks with the “ Montreal model .” The model combines ketamine with a therapeutic environment and weekly psychotherapy. Researchers found significant advancement in severely depressed patients. The approach views ketamine’s psychedelic effects as possibly beneficial. Can ketamine treat depression long-term? The innovative “Montreal model” for treating depression, which integrates ketamine with a therapeutic environment and weekly psychotherapy, shows promising results in extending ketamine’s antidepressant effects, according to a new study.
This is the first randomized clinical study of its kind to evaluate the effectiveness of the “Montreal model,” an increasingly utilized approach for treating resistant depression, ofen accompanied by suicidal thoughts. Dr. Nicolas Garel, a specialist at the CHUM research center , explained, “There were data that showed that the experience of ketamine, when you look at it with a therapeutic eye, could be potentially beneficial.”
Ketamine, an anesthetic, has been used to treat depression, and is sometimes considered the most important psychopharmacological revelation in the last thirty years. However, its effects typically fade within a week or two.
Did You Know? Ketamine was first synthesized in 1962 and initially used as an anesthetic for animals and humans during the Vietnam War. Researchers found that by incorporating ketamine into a therapeutic environment with weekly psychotherapy, some patients saw improvements in their symptoms up to eight weeks after treatment ended.
Dr. kyle Greenway from McGill , another study author, emphasized, “We are talking about extremely sick people… And even in this population, we show that ketamine has a fairly significant effect.” He noted that around 30 to 40% of severely depressed patients responded to this intervention.
The “Montreal model” views ketamine’s psychedelic effects and altered states of consciousness as potentially therapeutic, not simply side effects.”our approach is to look at the experience of dissociation not as a form of psychosis,but perhaps as something that has a therapeutic value,” said Dr. Greenway.
Researchers discovered that ketamine, administered within the context of the Montreal model, could provide significant benefits even at a dosage considered minimal in an anesthesia context. According to Dr. Greenway, ketamine can help patients experience their emotions more intensely during psychotherapy.
Dr. Garel noted that the rapid, albeit temporary, effect of ketamine in suffering patients “can lead them to get involved in a therapeutic process… Because when you are very suffering, it is tough to engage in a psychotherapeutic process.” Dr. Greenway added that the goal “it’s not to have a mystical experience, it’s to learn together what it means to take.”
Patients in the study experienced profound changes, according to Dr. Garel. “We saw them realize, having self-criticism processes, rediscovering a curiosity for themselves, for life, for others, returning to activities that had set aside for years as they were in a state of immobility, then of total loss of meaning,” he said.
The study provided quantitative data to support what Dr. Greenway and Dr. Garel had observed on an interpersonal level for years. Dr. Garel stated that the study demonstrated that the “profits have persisted over time.” Even a month after the final ketamine dose, the antidepressant, anti-pest, and anxiolytic response was “wholly maintained.”
Key Finding: The study showed that the positive effects of ketamine, when combined with therapy, can last for at least one month after the final dose. The Montreal model is currently being replicated and adapted in other parts of Quebec,as well as in various countries worldwide. The study’s findings were published in the British Journal of Psychiatry .
The Critical Role of psychotherapy with Ketamine The “Montreal model” underscores not just the potential of ketamine, but also the indispensable role of psychotherapy in depression treatment. While ketamine’s rapid action can offer immediate relief, it’s the integration of therapy that appears to facilitate long-term benefits, as the recent study highlights. This approach recognizes that ketamine is not a standalone cure but a catalyst for deeper therapeutic work.
The research showcases how combining ketamine with psychotherapy can extend its benefits significantly. This is not just about ketamine; it’s about using the drug to open a window for meaningful psychological change. By providing a safe and supportive environment, therapists can guide patients through the emotional experiences triggered by ketamine, fostering understanding and coping mechanisms.
Here’s how psychotherapy supports the therapeutic process:
Emotional Processing: Psychotherapy helps patients unpack and understand the emotions that surface during ketamine treatment. Behavioral Changes: Therapy provides tools to address the behaviors and thought patterns that contribute to depression. Building Resilience: Regular sessions equip patients with strategies to cope with future challenges. Maintaining Gains: Consistent therapy reinforces the positive changes experienced during ketamine treatment. The supportive environment created by therapists is just as crucial as the ketamine itself. It offers a structured space for patients to explore their inner world, process difficult emotions, and develop healthier coping strategies. The ultimate goal is to help patients gain long-term mental well-being beyond the direct effects of the medication.
Vital Point: Ketamine is fast acting, but its effects by themselves are temporary. The added element of psychotherapy is vital to help improve the ability to get better for the long term.
The “Montreal model” demonstrates that while ketamine can be a powerful tool, it is most effective when used as one component of a comprehensive treatment plan. This model’s success prompts further examination of the effects of therapeutic integration, which means a re-evaluation of the roles of both medication and therapeutic support in the treatment of depression.
Many patients are exploring the use of ketamine for treatment-resistant depression: Ketamine can be a viable option, and in specific situations, is the best option, for treatment-resistant depression. In cases from other studies where other treatments haven’t worked (like citalopram/Celexa), the FDA has approved medication that uses esketamine to help improve the patient’s mental state. [[3]] though, it is indeed critically important that each patient collaborates with a medical professional before starting such a treatment.
Practical Considerations for Ketamine and therapy If you or someone you know is considering ketamine for depression, here are some practical considerations:
Find a Qualified Professional: Seek a psychiatrist or therapist experienced in ketamine-assisted psychotherapy. Discuss Your Medical History: Share your complete medical and psychiatric history to ensure ketamine is appropriate. Understand the Treatment Process: Clarify the treatment protocol, including dosage, frequency, and integration therapy sessions. Prepare for the Experience: Learn about potential side effects and how to manage them, including the possibility of dissociation and altered perceptions. Commit to Therapy: Be prepared to engage actively in regular psychotherapy sessions before, during, and after treatment. Set Realistic Expectations: Understand that ketamine may not be a cure-all, and it may take time to experience lasting benefits. The integration of ketamine and therapy is a complex process that requires careful planning and execution. By working with qualified professionals and understanding what to expect, patients can maximize their chances of achieving positive outcomes.
Ketamine and Therapy: Myths vs. Facts As ketamine gains more attention,it’s important to dispel some common myths:
Myth Fact ketamine is a fast fix for depression. Ketamine can provide rapid relief, but lasting benefits typically require psychotherapy and a comprehensive treatment plan. Ketamine is only for severe cases. ketamine’s use can vary, being used in severe or treatment resistant cases depending on the patient needs, and as a part of a larger process of treatment. Ketamine is addictive. Ketamine carries some risk, but when administered within a supervised therapeutic setting, the risk of addiction is substantially reduced. Ketamine alone is enough. In most cases, combining ketamine with psychotherapy and a supportive environment, like the Montreal model, yields more robust and durable results. Frequently Asked questions About Ketamine Treatment Here are a few common questions about using ketamine for depression:
What is the role of psychotherapy in ketamine treatment? Psychotherapy offers a framework for processing emotional experiences, developing coping mechanisms, and integrating positive changes stimulated by ketamine.
Who is a good candidate for ketamine treatment? people with treatment-resistant depression, those experiencing suicidal thoughts, or those who have not responded to customary antidepressants are ofen considered. [[1]]
Are there any side effects? Common side effects include nausea, dissociation, increased blood pressure, and temporary cognitive changes. These are generally manageable in a clinical setting.
